title: The Power of Price
coreMove: Separate the price signal from the result before letting expensive become synonymous with effective.
sourcePressure: The source shows that price can change expected and even experienced effectiveness, as with placebo-like responses to discounted versus full-price products.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The weak version says expensive is not always better; the precise lesson is that price can become an active expectation that alters perceived results.

hook: The expensive one works before it works

exampleSpecs.domain: running-store insole fitting with covered prices
exampleSpecs.audience: a recreational runner choosing between insoles before a half marathon
exampleSpecs.stakes: buying the most expensive pair because the price makes support feel stronger
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the fitter covers the price stickers and has the runner jog the hallway before ranking knee comfort
exampleSpecs.firstImage: three insole pairs lined on a rubber mat with tape over the price stickers

exampleSpecs.domain: music producer testing budget and premium plug-ins
exampleSpecs.audience: a producer mixing a vocal track under deadline
exampleSpecs.stakes: hearing quality because the premium plug-in window looks expensive
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: a collaborator renames the plug-ins A and B, bounces both mixes, and asks the producer to choose before seeing the price
exampleSpecs.firstImage: two audio tracks labeled A and B on a glowing mix screen

exampleSpecs.domain: pet owner comparing flea treatments after a coupon
exampleSpecs.audience: a dog owner doubting a discounted treatment before the vet visit
exampleSpecs.stakes: misreading ordinary scratching as product failure because discount lowered confidence
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the vet covers the receipt total and asks the owner to track actual flea counts on the comb before judging effectiveness
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a flea comb on a paper exam-table sheet beside a folded receipt

exampleSpecs.domain: language-learning app offered through an employer discount
exampleSpecs.audience: an employee deciding whether the discounted app is weaker than the full-price competitor
exampleSpecs.stakes: abandoning useful practice because lower price feels like lower learning power
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the employee hides subscription prices and compares two weeks of completed speaking drills instead of prestige
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a phone showing completed speaking drills beside a benefits enrollment page

exampleSpecs.domain: barber shop testing house-made hair product
exampleSpecs.audience: a barber deciding whether clients believe the unlabeled jar works
exampleSpecs.stakes: mistaking packaging price cues for hold and shine
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the barber fills identical tins from premium and house batches, marks them only by color dots, and checks which style holds by closing time
exampleSpecs.firstImage: identical silver tins lined below a mirror with tiny color dots

exampleSpecs.audience: a library director choosing chairs for staff workstations
exampleSpecs.stakes: assuming the expensive chair reduces pain before staff try unlabeled models
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: after a week of covered labels and rotation logs, the director compares reported back comfort to chair codes rather than catalog prices
exampleSpecs.firstImage: chair catalog pages tucked under a checkout-desk keyboard tray

skillTargets: identify price as an expectancy cue
distinguish true quality differences from price-induced confidence
evaluate discount effects on perceived effectiveness

tryThisNowSpec: Before judging whether a paid tool or product worked, hide the price and write one observable result you can compare without knowing what it cost.
